name: In-process caches
summary: A small cache inside your service’s own memory: no network hop, but every copy of the service has its own.
howItWorks: An in-process cache is a map kept in the same memory as your code, with rules for what to throw away. You look a key up, and on a miss you compute or fetch the value and store it for next time. Because it’s an ordinary memory lookup, a hit takes nanoseconds to a few microseconds, with no network call, no serialisation and nothing extra to run. Memory is limited, so the cache evicts entries: **LRU** drops the least recently used, Caffeine’s **W-TinyLFU** also weighs how often a key has been used, and a **TTL** expires entries after a fixed time so stale data can’t live forever. Libraries handle this for you: Caffeine or Guava in Java, `lru-cache` in Node, `functools.lru_cache` in Python, `IMemoryCache` in .NET. The catch is that each running instance has its own cache. With ten pods there are ten copies, each warming up separately after a deploy, each using memory counted against that pod’s limit, and each possibly holding a different version of the same record. Clearing a key in one pod leaves the other nine stale until their TTL runs out, unless you broadcast invalidations. That’s why in-process caches suit data that is read often, changes rarely and may be slightly stale, and why many systems put one in front of a shared cache such as Valkey or Redis: **two-level caching**, where the local cache absorbs the hottest keys and the shared one keeps all instances close to each other and protects the database.
analogy: A sticky note on your own monitor versus the team whiteboard. Reading your note is instant, but when the meeting time changes, everyone’s notes are wrong until each person rewrites theirs; the whiteboard is a walk away, but there’s only one of it.
useWhen: Hot, small, read-mostly data: configuration, feature flags, currency rates, product categories, compiled templates
Results that are expensive to compute and safe to be a little stale for seconds or minutes
As the first level in front of a shared cache, to cut network round trips for the hottest keys
Memoising a pure function inside one process
avoidWhen: Data that must look the same on every instance right after a write, such as account balances or permissions just revoked
Large datasets: every instance pays the memory, and a big cache can push a pod over its memory limit
Sessions or anything a user expects to follow them across instances, unless you pin users to instances
example: A pricing service runs on eight pods. Each keeps the 10,000 most-used product records in Caffeine for 30 seconds, behind a shared Valkey cache with a five-minute TTL. On a hit the pod answers without a network call; a miss on the pod costs one Valkey round trip, and only a miss in both reaches the database. When a price changes, the service deletes the Valkey key, and the pods catch up within 30 seconds, which the business has agreed is acceptable for list prices.

story: Remembering a function’s answers is older than web caches. In April 1968 Donald Michie described “memo” functions in Nature: functions that keep a record of results they have already computed, the idea now called memoisation. Application code kept doing it too, holding hot data in a local variable or a map.

The web exposed the limits. In 2004 Brad Fitzpatrick explained why he wrote memcached for LiveJournal: each of the 30 to 50 mod_perl processes on a web server had its own address space and could cache only for itself, which wasted memory, and he didn’t want 40-plus machines all caching independently and duplicating the same data. A shared cache over the network fixed that, and for years the in-process cache was the less fashionable option.

It came back as a first level in front of shared caches, because even a fast network cache costs a round trip. Libraries made it easy: Python 3.2 added `functools.lru_cache` in 2011, Guava added `CacheBuilder` the same year, and Ben Manes, who had worked on Guava’s cache, went on to write Caffeine, using the W-TinyLFU policy from a 2015 paper he wrote with Gil Einziger and Roy Friedman. Redis 6 (2020) added server-assisted client-side caching, which tells clients when keys they cached locally have changed, and .NET’s HybridCache (2025) packaged two-level caching with stampede protection.

choices.choice: Keep the cache in the same process as the code
choices.why: Access to local memory is orders of magnitude faster than a networked service, as Redis’s own documentation on client-side caching points out, and there is no extra system to run.

choices.choice: Bound the cache by size and by time
choices.why: An unbounded map is a memory leak. lru-cache refuses to start without max, maxSize or ttl, and .NET leaves the size limit to the developer because the runtime won’t shrink the cache under memory pressure.

choices.choice: Weigh frequency as well as recency
choices.why: Plain LRU lets a burst of one-off keys push out entries that are used all the time. TinyLFU keeps a compact frequency sketch and admits a new entry only if it is likely to be used more than the one it would evict.

choices.choice: Put a shared cache behind it
choices.why: Per-instance caches disagree and each warms up on its own. A shared second level keeps instances close to each other and protects the database, while the local level absorbs the hottest keys.
